reading.source_scope_note: A controlled laboratory task presents live human/Pepper actions through a switchable transparent screen. Reported analysis uses55 young adults from a160-person project,with trained explicit High/Low agency/experience choices plus timing/mouse trajectories. The RW-IAT name does not itself validate unconscious associations,dimensional structure or field generality.
access_limits: All supplied text,three figures and complete bibliography read. ACM public HTML retrieval returned403; no additional appendix,data,code,preregistration or task implementation obtained.

The full160-person cohort,the438-person action norming studies and274-person lexical norming study are described through other project reports,not independently analyzed or counted as new samples in this55-person result.

Original IAT,SingleCategoryIAT,MP-IAT,mouse-tracking and cited software/naturalism sources are not independently fully read from the bibliography. Metadata repair does not provide independent paper credit.

No raw responses,precise condition means,trajectory normalization details,full posthoc matrices or reliability/criterion-validity estimates supplied. Graphs support directions,not exact recovered raw estimates.

study.participants: Project160adults,18–73,four generations. This report deliberately presents55participants18–35,mean25.93,SD5.59,33women,to align with conventional age ranges and earlier workN53. These55are a subset,not an additional160 or explained105-person dropout. Bilkent ethics approval,consent andapproximately3USDcompensation stated.
study.norming: Forty human/robot action animations/video candidates were normed by438participants across two earlier online studies; four communicative and four noncommunicative actions selected using recognition/confidence/category ratings,entropy and clustering. Lexical concepts were normed by274in separate prior work. Shared-project reports should not be treated as independent replications automatically.
study.apparatus: Human actor and Pepper robot perform live actions behind a55inch OLED screen that switches transparent for six-second actions and opaque for instructions/responses. Curtains,backstage control,camera,music and lighting standardize transitions. This is a live laboratory/Wizard-of-Oz setup,not an uncontrolled field experiment or proof of autonomous robot performance.
study.training: Participants learn explicit agency/experience definitions and High/Low categories to80%accuracy,then identify the eight actions. This standardizes task meaning but can shape later judgments; it does not independently discover the number of mental-capacity dimensions.
study.task: Four counterbalanced blocks,RobotAgency,RobotExperience,HumanAgency,HumanExperience,each with eight actions in randomized order. Participants explicitly click High/Low capacity after each action,encouraged to be fast/instinctive. Mouse latency,maximum deviation and area under trajectory are additional indirect process measures. No standard congruent/incongruent pairing contrast or D-score is reported.
study.analysis: Participant condition averages used after eight trial outliers;1750trials reported. Friedman tests followed by Nemenyi posthoc comparisons. Actor and action main contrasts reported separately for each dimension/outcome; no full actor×action interaction or overall multiplicity policy provided.
study.agency_results: Robot receives a higher HighAgency response proportion than human,while actor RT/MD/AUC differences are nonsignificant. Communicative actions increase agency response time and trajectory deviations,without a significant HighAgency proportion contrast. These can reflect task-specific capacity requirements or expectations rather than a universal robot superiority judgment.
study.experience_results: Robot elicits slower responses,more trajectory deviation and lower HighExperience proportions than human. Communicative actions yield more HighExperience choices than noncommunicative actions,without significant action effects on RT/MD/AUC. Separate significant/nonsignificant results do not establish cross-dimension interactions.
study.interpretation: Lowered robot expectations are suggested using spontaneous comments,not directly manipulated/measured as a mediator. Mouse curvature and response time can reflect decision difficulty,motor demands or learned response mapping as well as hesitation; they do not uniquely identify unconscious beliefs or actual mental capacities.

trial_accounting.boundary: Two further missing/excluded trials or another count basis may explain the difference; none is documented here,so do not invent a repair.

study.test_boundary: Selected standard tails agree with reported main-test thresholds. Different Nemenyi posthoc p values are not automatically reporting errors; exact comparison family/output unavailable.

findings.definition: Ascribing or denying mental capacities to another entity.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing capacity-attribution construct; add a live laboratory operationalization and measurement limits rather than invent another behavior from an instrument name.
findings.evidence_scope: Live human and Pepper actions are classified by participants on trained High/Low agency/experience labels,with time and mouse trajectories recorded. This broadens measurement context beyond image/text studies,but does not validate unconscious mind attribution or a universal dimensional architecture.
findings.boundary: Explicit choices and indirect process indices differ. The method’s name,live robot presence and fast responses do not by themselves establish ecological validity,automaticity,actual robot mentality or general field behavior.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity a capacity for intentional thought, planning and action.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing capacity-attribution construct; add a live laboratory operationalization and measurement limits rather than invent another behavior from an instrument name.

evidence.quote: High Agency responses for the robot actor

findings.evidence_scope: In the selected55-person analysis,robot actions produce a higher HighAgency response ratio than human actions,while actor timing/trajectory contrasts are nonsignificant. Action type affects time/trajectory metrics,not the agency ratio. Interpretation concerns required capacity under task instructions.
findings.boundary: No general claim that robots are more agentic than humans. Expectations,task framing,movement differences and explicit conceptual training can affect judgments; the expectation account is not a demonstrated mediator.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity the capacity for subjective feelings or sensations, such as pleasure, pain, fear or joy.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing capacity-attribution construct; add a live laboratory operationalization and measurement limits rather than invent another behavior from an instrument name.
findings.evidence_scope: Human actions receive higher HighExperience proportions than robot actions;communicative actions higher than noncommunicative. Robot evaluations also take longer and show more trajectory deviation. The outcomes are perception/task response measures.
findings.boundary: No actual feeling,sentience or moral-worth measurement. Learned labels do not establish independently separable experience factors; longer mouse trajectories do not prove a unique unconscious conflict.

findings.definition: Attributing human characteristics, intentions, emotions or other mental states to a nonhuman entity.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing capacity-attribution construct; add a live laboratory operationalization and measurement limits rather than invent another behavior from an instrument name.
findings.evidence_scope: The report motivates a live embodied-human/robot task with prior anthropomorphism literature and observes context-specific capacity attributions. It does not randomize physical versus virtual embodiment or independently measure all humanlike-trait attributions.
findings.boundary: Presence,behavior,perceived capacity and actual humanlike mind differ. A live laboratory task is not evidence that embodiment necessarily improves real-world trust or human welfare.

findings.definition: Inferring another’s beliefs, intentions, desires or emotions to explain or anticipate their behavior.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing capacity-attribution construct; add a live laboratory operationalization and measurement limits rather than invent another behavior from an instrument name.
findings.evidence_scope: Mental-state attribution and intentional stance motivate the task,but participants judge general required agency/experience,not the accuracy of a particular belief/intent inference.
findings.boundary: Capacity classification and accurate mentalizing are related but distinct. No new independent theory-of-mind performance paper credit follows from this background discussion.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: 55participants×four blocks×eight actions=1760potential trials. Removing eight outliers leaves1752,rather than reported1750. Missing trials or another count basis may explain the difference; raw logs/exclusion accounting unavailable.

Participants deliberately classify capacity using trained definitions. Timing/mouse measures may offer indirect process information,but no independent automaticity/unconscious-association criterion is established here. The authors themselves call for further validation; do not call the method meaningless or its latent interpretation proven.

methodological_limits: Selected young subset from a larger project and live lab setting; no representative cohort or field generalization demonstrated.
Extensive lexical/action training can influence responses. Using two predetermined dimensions is not a test that two dimensions are universally correct.
Implicit task title,quick answers and motor trajectories do not uniquely identify unconscious association,strength of belief or actual mind. Standard IAT compatibility scoring is not reported.
Multiple outcomes/main contrasts,limited interaction/output reporting and unresolved trial counts constrain fine-grained inference; selected chi-square thresholds are arithmetically consistent.
Physical-presence benefit and changed expectations are not independently randomized mediators; actor/action comparisons need stimulus and task scope.
Prior project norming studies and full160-person data are not extra independent sample support for this reported55-person analysis.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Changing response format or adding behavior metrics does not erase conceptual training or prior knowledge. Here High/Low definitions are explicitly learned before the task.
Predetermined agency/experience classification is compatible with studying those concepts,but does not refute alternative aggregate factor solutions or validate universal dimensions.
Response speed and cognitive-process labels need validation. A fast answer or mouse curvature is not a direct readout of an unconscious mechanism or AI mentality.
